pages.x: Britain bought huge amounts of Chinese tea, but China wanted little that Britain made, so silver drained east. The answer the British East India Company found was opium, grown in India and smuggled into China through Canton. By the 1830s millions of Chinese were addicted, and silver was flowing out of China instead.

In 1839 the emperor sent an upright official, Lin Zexu, to Canton to stamp out the trade. Lin shut in the foreign merchants until they handed over more than 1,000 tonnes of opium, then had it mixed with lime and salt and washed out to sea at Humen. He even wrote to Queen Victoria asking how she would like her own people poisoned.

Britain sent warships. The iron steamship Nemesis sailed up shallow rivers and blew Chinese war junks to pieces. British forces took the forts of Canton, then sailed up the Yangtze and threatened Nanjing. China's armies, with old guns and older tactics, could not stop them.

In 1842 China signed the first of what Chinese call the unequal treaties. It paid Britain millions of silver dollars, opened five ports to British trade and gave up the island of Hong Kong, which Britain ruled until 1997. The opium trade carried on, bigger than ever.

In 1856 Chinese officials boarded the Arrow, a ship flying the British flag, and Britain, now joined by France, went to war again. Their forces took Canton and the forts guarding Tianjin, and in 1858 China agreed to open more ports, let foreign ships use its rivers, let missionaries travel and, at last, to make opium legal.

When China held out, British and French troops marched on Beijing in 1860. Envoys sent to talk were seized, and many of them died after torture. In revenge the British commander, Lord Elgin, had the emperor's Garden of Perfect Brightness looted and burned. It took thousands of soldiers two days, and smoke hung over the city.

The wars showed that the Qing empire, the richest in the world a century before, could not defend itself against industrial Europe. Chinese call 1839 to 1949 the century of humiliation, and it still colours how China sees the West. Lin Zexu is a national hero, and the world day against drugs, 26 June, recalls his work at Humen.
pts: Lin Zexu destroyed the opium at Humen, 1839
Hong Kong was given up to Britain in 1842
The Summer Palace was burned in 1860
The start of a century of humiliation
